research_concepts: shot mix shift due to personnel change
offensive five composition and shot selection
detecting causal lineup effects through shot mix
methodological validation using shot mix as a test statistic
methodological_questions: Is shot mix change a reliable indicator of personnel effect, given variation in shot type stability?
What sample size (possessions per lineup) is needed to detect meaningful shot mix differences?
How can opponent lineup, game state, and team strategy be controlled to isolate offensive personnel?
Does observational lineup variation (coach decisions) produce detectable shot mix changes in this dataset?
Are there previous attempts to use shot mix to validate lineup effect detection that failed?
evidence_establishes: No historical evidence was available; nothing is pre-established for this specific question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a shot-mix-based test can detect offensive five effects with sufficient power and control in these data.
What the appropriate lineup-level sample size threshold should be.
The degree of confounding by opponent quality and game context.
The reliability of any previous implementation of this design.
own_inferences: The data contain play-by-play shot distance and derived play-type possessions, so shot mix (e.g., three-point proportion, rim frequency) can be constructed for each offensive lineup.
With three full seasons, many lineups will accumulate hundreds of possessions, but rarer five-man combos will still suffer from small samples and sparse exposure.
Lineup changes are endogenous: coaches adjust personnel in response to score, matchups, rest, and hot/cold streaks. Simple before/after comparisons are likely confounded.
If the true effect of personnel on shot mix is modest, the signal may be swamped by noise, opponent effects, and game-state shifts.
A validation study of this sort could over-interpret statistically significant differences that are actually artifacts of multiple testing or label noise in the derived play types.
uncertainties: The exact structure and accuracy of the derived play-type possession records (e.g., how reliably initiator, play type, and points are assigned).
The granularity of the defensive matchup data (possession-level or segment-level) and whether it accurately captures who guarded whom.
Whether the research team intends a within-team, cross-team, or league-wide comparison.
The pre-specified minimum effect size they would consider ‘detectable’ for a design validation.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieval returned no earlier studies, so the decision is based solely on the research question, data description, and methodological assessment.

blocking_constraints.text: Many five-man lineups will have too few possessions for reliable shot-mix estimates; sparsity erodes power.
Non-random lineup selection by coaches correlates with opponent strength, game situation, and recent performance, confounding shot-mix comparisons.
Comparing shot-mix across hundreds of lineups inflates false positives unless multiplicity adjustments are pre-registered.
Derived play-type records depend on a model or rule-based assignment; misclassification of play types or initiators can create spurious shot-mix differences.

prior_work.summary: No previous work on this specific question was retrieved; the design appears novel within this project.

risks.text: Lineups with low possession counts (e.g., < 100) produce unstable shot-mix estimates; power to detect meaningful differences is low for many combos.
A large fraction of possible offensive fives appears only in garbage time or due to foul trouble, leading to very few observations and extreme selection.

Changes in offensive five are often paired with changes in the opponent’s defensive five and with score-driven tactical shifts, making it hard to attribute shot-mix changes to the offensive personnel alone.
Testing many lineups without a correction plan risks false discovery; a league-wide omnibus test is safer but less informative about specific combos.
The shot mix depends on play-type labels that may be mis-assigned, particularly ambiguous transition vs. half-court designs, creating correlated errors that could mimic lineup effects.
Shot distance bins or play-type groupings may not be stable within a lineup over small samples, leading to spurious ‘differences’ from a handful of possessions.

design.estimand: The difference in shot-type distribution (e.g., % three-point, % rim, % mid-range) between two offensive five-man lineups of the same team, holding opponent defensive lineup strength and game context constant.
design.unit: A possession with a specific offensive five, linked to the defensive five and period/score state.
design.sample: All offensive lineups from the 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 regular seasons that logged at least 300 non-garbage-time possessions. Garbage time defined as last 5 minutes of 4th quarter with score margin > 15.
design.power: Using simulation, determine the minimum number of possessions per lineup needed to detect a 5-percentage-point shift in three-point attempt rate at 80 % power, alpha = 0.01, adjusting for within-team correlation. Exclude lineups below that threshold.
design.controls: Fixed effects for opponent defensive lineup (clustered by similarity), game location (home/away), period, point differential at start of possession, and indicator for back-to-back game.
design.falsification: 1) Permutation test: shuffle shot mixes across lineups within the same team and check that the observed differences are no longer detectable. 2) Stability test: split each lineup’s possessions into odd/even games and confirm shot mix correlates at r > 0.7.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a hierarchical testing plan: first an omnibus chi-square test comparing all lineups against the team average; only if significant, apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction to pairwise comparisons among top-20 most-used lineups.
design.decision_rule: The design is deemed to detect personnel effects if (a) the omnibus test rejects the null of equal distributions at p < 0.001, and (b) at least 60 % of previously defined high-minutes lineups show a significant pairwise difference after multiplicity correction.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score summary as of 2026-11-02; derived play-type possession records from the project's graph database (version commit hash pre-registered).

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to parse the research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." The researcher is asking: if we change the five players on the floor (substitutions), does the team's shot mix (distribution of shot types, locations, etc.) change? They want to see if their experimental design can detect personnel effects.

Data: play-by-play with shot distance and result, substitutions, starters, defensive matchups, box score, derived play-type possessions (initiator, play type, points). So we can identify when the offensive five changes, and then look at shot characteristics (e.g., three-point rate, mid-range frequency, shot distance distribution) in possessions before/after or between different five-man units. The question is about whether they can detect a signal that changing the personnel directly alters shot mix (as opposed to being due to opponent defense, game state, etc.). So it's a methodological study to validate a design.

We need to retrieve history. I need to formulate research concepts: maybe "lineup changes", "shot mix", "personnel effects", "offensive five variation", "detecting causal effects". Methodological questions: "Is shot mix sensitive to lineup changes?", "Can we detect personnel effects with observational data?", "Confounding by opponent, score, or substitution timing?", "Sample size for lineup-level analysis?" etc.

But the retrieval tool expects three args: research_concepts (list), methodological_questions (list), and query (string). I'll craft them.

I'll set research_concepts: ["lineup effect on shot distribution", "shot mix shift due to personnel change", "offensive five composition and shot selection", "detecting causal lineup effects", "methodological validation with shot mix"].

methodological_questions: ["Is shot mix change a reliable indicator of personnel effect?", "What sample size is needed per lineup?", "How to control for opponent and game state confounders?", "Does observational lineup variation produce detectable shot mix changes?", "Are there previous attempts that failed?"]

query: "changing offensive five shot mix design detection personnel effects"

Now call retrieve_history.

We are in stage 2. The retrieval result is empty: no historical evidence available. So we must now assess the research question based on the data description and tools. We need to fill out the schema.

First, let's parse the research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." This seems to be a methodological validation question: they want to check if when you change the five players on the court (the offensive lineup), does the shot distribution (shot mix) change? And if so, that demonstrates the research design is capable of detecting personnel effects. Essentially, a sanity check: if different lineups have different shot mixes, then the data and analysis can pick up lineup-specific effects. The question is whether this can be tested with the available data: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 seasons (regular + playoffs), per-game play-by-play with substitutions, defensive matchups, etc., plus derived play-type possession records.

We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions, based on the task statement and data. The concepts: lineup effect on shot distribution, shot mix shift due to personnel change, etc. Methodological questions: Is shot mix change a reliable indicator? Sample size per lineup? Confounders? etc. We'll list them in the output.

Historical evidence: empty list because no records returned. So historical_evidence: [], failed_approaches: []. evidence_establishes: what the retrieved evidence establishes (nothing, as no evidence). evidence_does_not_establish: everything left open. own_inferences: what we infer from domain knowledge and data description. uncertainties: what we don't know. historical_effect: changed_decision: "no_historical_evidence", explanation accordingly.

Now testability: assess whether the question can be answered with these data. Blocking constraints: list risk codes that are likely to make it difficult. The question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix". It's a causal claim: when you change the offensive lineup, shot mix changes. To test this, you'd compare shot distributions across lineups. Need to define shot mix: perhaps distribution of shot types (e.g., three-point vs. mid-range vs. paint, or play types). Data includes play-by-play with shot distance and result, and derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). So shot mix can be operationalized. You'd need enough lineup observations. Sample size: per-game data over three seasons provides many lineups, but each specific five-man combo may have limited minutes. There's a risk of small sample sizes for many combinations, leading to insufficient power. Also, confounding: lineup changes are not random; coaches choose lineups based on game situation, opposing lineups, injuries, etc. So any observed shot mix difference could be due to game state, opponent defensive strength, etc. The question says "showing the design can detect personnel effects." It seems like a validation that the analysis pipeline works. Possibly they want to use something like a lineup-based shot chart analysis. Might be testable with enough data and appropriate controls, but there are risks.

Risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (low minutes for many lineups), CONFOUNDING (selection bias, opponent adjustments), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (how to categorize shot mix reliably, stability of shot types over small samples), MULTIPLE_TESTING (if comparing many lineups). EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: some lineups appear rarely. Also LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD? Not likely if using within-game data. RTM_SELECTION: if lineups are selected based on recent performance. OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: shot mix might be an outcome derived from play-by-play that itself depends on labeling play types, which could have errors. So I'll list those risks.

Now predicted_outcome: probability distribution. I'd lean that the question as posed is somewhat vague: "changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix" – do they mean any change in any lineup results in a different shot mix? That might be over broad. But maybe they just want to demonstrate that the design (which includes data and analysis) can detect known differences in shot distributions between lineups, as a proof of concept. I'd say it's testable with appropriate methods, but there is a chance of artifact (e.g., detecting difference due to opponent rather than offensive personnel). Probability of supported: if they do a well-designed comparison (e.g., within-team, same opponent strength, controlling for game state), they may find that different lineups have different shot mixes, which is plausible because different players have different shot preferences. So supported high. But if they find no difference, it might be due to low power, so "rejected" low. "untestable" moderate because of the difficulty in establishing causal effect of the offensive five alone without random assignment. "artifact" moderate if not controlling for opponent. "uncertain" covers inconclusive. I'll assign: supported 0.4, rejected 0.1, untestable 0.2, artifact 0.2, uncertain 0.1.

Decision: proceed_with_changes because the research question needs clearer specification and careful design to control confounders, but the data likely allow it. Or do_not_proceed if I think it's too difficult. I'll go with proceed_with_changes, suggesting more precise estimand, control for opponent and game state, adequate sample size threshold.

Design: estimand: the effect of swapping offensive five-man lineups (within the same team) on the distribution of shot types (e.g., proportion of three-point attempts, rim attempts, etc.) in a possession, holding opponent defensive lineup and game context constant. Unit: possession or game segment with a specific offensive lineup. Sample: all lineups from the 2022-23 to 2024-25 seasons that have at least 200 possessions together (or some threshold). Power: compute minimum detectable effect size based on lineup minutes. Controls: opponent defensive lineup strength (using defensive matchup data), game score differential, period, home/away, and team fixed effects. Falsification: test that if you randomly reassign lineups to shot mix, any detected effect disappears; also check that within-lineup shot mix is stable across different opponents. Multiplicity: correct for multiple lineup comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg or focus on pre-defined lineups. Decision rule: if a significant difference in shot mix (via chi-squared test on shot categories) is found for a majority of lineups after adjustment, conclude the design detects personnel effects. Data version: specify the exact data pulls.

I'll now fill out the JSON. Note: historical_effect explanation will note that no historical evidence was retrieved. prior_work.already_answered: unknown, cited empty list, summary "No prior work on this exact question was retrieved."

Let's write the response.
